chunks: We were told by my father, may Allah grant him mercy, that he said: We were told by Muhammad ibn Yahya al-‘Attar, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Ash‘ari, from al-‘Abbas ibn Ma‘ruf, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Maskan, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
with regards to the saying of Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He: «Allah has not instituted baheera, nor sa’iba, nor waseela, nor haam.»

He said: Indeed, the people of the Jahiliya, when a female camel gave birth to two children in one belly, they would say: «She connected» and they would not consider it allowable to slaughter it, nor eat it. If she gave birth to ten, they would make it a sa’iba, and they would not permit its back nor to eat it. The haam is the male camel which they did not consider allowable. Then Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, sent down that He had not forbidden anything of that.

key_terms.بَحِيرَة: A camel whose ears were cut to be exempt from work and slaughter
key_terms.حَامّ: A male camel exempt from work
key_terms.سَائِبَة: A camel set free to graze without being tended
key_terms.وَصِيلَة: A camel connected to another by releasing one in place of the other

ai.seo_question: What were the pre-Islamic camel customs of baheera, sa'iba, wasila, and haam mentioned in the Quran?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this narration to clarify the specific pre-Islamic Arabian customs of designating camels as sacred, noting that 'baheera,' 'sa'iba,' 'wasila,' and 'haam' were arbitrary human inventions rather than divine decrees. The Imam explains that Allah revealed these practices were not originally instituted by Him, thereby abrogating the Jahiliyyah superstitions and establishing that the prohibition was merely cultural, not religious.
